source_paper.title: The Effect of Increasing Nickel Content on the Microstructure, Hardness, and Corrosion Resistance of the CuFeTiZrNix High-Entropy Alloys.

hypotheses.builds_on: This hypothesis builds on the observation in PMC9104004 that the distribution and evolution of intermetallic phases significantly affect corrosion performance. It extends the concept by using a localized, laser-based processing technique to purposely refine the microstructure and control elemental distribution.
hypotheses.what_is_new: The proposal of using laser surface remelting to engineer a nano-scale, homogeneous precipitate distribution that suppresses active Cu-rich regions and thereby enhances protective oxide scale formation in a lightweight Mg-containing HEA is a novel processing strategy not previously reported.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Laser surface remelting (LSR) applied to the as-cast MgAlCuZnGd HEA will create an ultrafine, non-equilibrium surface microstructure characterized by nanometer-scale, uniformly distributed intermetallic precipitates. This refined microstructure minimizes the formation of large, Cu-rich regions, leading to the development of a more uniform and protective oxide scale during high-temperature exposure, and thereby improving corrosion resistance.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: A metastable, as-cast MgAlCuZnGd high-entropy alloy exhibiting heterogeneous microstructure with coarse intermetallic phases and a relatively uniform, but supersaturated, Cu distribution.
hypothesis.intervention: Employ laser surface remelting on the top ~200–300 µm of the as-cast alloy using controlled laser power and scan speeds to achieve rapid local melting and solidification.
hypothesis.conditions: Following LSR, subject the treated samples to high-temperature oxidation at 600 °C in air and undertake corrosion testing in a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: The rapid solidification from LSR produces a nanostructured surface layer with a finely dispersed distribution of intermetallic precipitates, which helps in curtailing macroscopic Cu segregation and suppresses regions prone to initiating pitting corrosion.
hypothesis.mechanism: The extremely high cooling rates in LSR result in an ultrafine microstructure where intermetallic precipitates form at the nanoscale. These finely distributed precipitates hinder the diffusion and agglomeration of Cu into larger, more reactive clusters. With a more homogeneous distribution of alloying elements, the surface is better able to form continuous, adherent oxide films (predominantly MgO and Al2O3) rather than discontinuous Cu-rich oxides. This modification reduces localized defects that serve as corrosion initiation sites.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated samples, LSR-treated specimens should exhibit (i) a markedly refined surface grain structure and reduced Cu-rich segregation (confirmed by TEM/EBSD and EDS), (ii) a more uniform and coherent oxide scale (assessed by cross-sectional SEM and XPS), and (iii) lower corrosion current densities plus a more noble corrosion potential from Tafel polarization measurements. The improvements are expected to be moderate and measurable.
hypothesis.baseline: An as-cast MgAlCuZnGd alloy with a conventional, coarser microstructure that tends to form heterogeneous, Cu-rich intermetallic regions.
hypothesis.boundary: The LSR parameters (laser power, scan rate, and remelt depth) must be optimized to avoid introducing thermal stresses, cracks, or other surface defects while ensuring sufficient microstructural refinement. The treatment is effective only in the remelted surface layer (~200–300 µm).
hypothesis.uncertainty: The extent to which LSR can homogenize the distribution of Cu and control intermetallic precipitate size in this complex HEA is not fully established, and the depth of the beneficial layer may be limited.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of samples: one set as-cast (baseline) and one set subjected to optimized laser surface remelting. Characterize the surface microstructure using TEM/EBSD and EDS mapping to assess precipitate size and Cu distribution. Perform high-temperature oxidation tests at 600 °C and corrosion tests in 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution with subsequent analysis of oxide scale uniformity (SEM/XPS) and electrochemical behavior (Tafel polarization).
measurements: Surface grain size and intermetallic precipitate distribution (TEM/EBSD, EDS)
Surface oxide scale uniformity and composition (SEM, XPS)
Corrosion metrics (corrosion current density and potential from Tafel analysis)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the LSR-treated samples do not exhibit a significant refinement of the surface microstructure and a reduction in Cu segregation, or if the oxide scale and corrosion metrics do not show measurable improvements over the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C10

source_paper.title: Characterisation of a Novel Complex Concentrated Alloy for Marine Applications.

hypotheses.builds_on: the paper’s demonstration that microstructural heterogeneity influences corrosion behavior, combined with principles of rapid solidification for grain refinement known from laser processing literature.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces a surface-specific intervention (laser remelting) to modify the microstructure, a processing technique not utilized in the paper, offering a new route to control corrosion and oxidation by tailoring only the alloy’s exterior microstructure.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Laser surface remelting of the as-cast Mg-containing high-entropy alloy generates a refined, near-surface microstructure with diminished coarse intermetallic segregation, thereby reducing microgalvanic effects and promoting the rapid formation of a uniform, adherent oxide scale that enhances both corrosion resistance and high-temperature oxidation performance.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: An as-cast non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy characterized by coarse dendritic regions and segregated interdendritic intermetallic networks.
hypothesis.intervention: Apply selective laser surface remelting to only the top ~50–100 µm of the alloy surface immediately after casting. Optimize laser parameters to induce rapid solidification that refines the surface microstructure without significantly altering the bulk.
hypothesis.conditions: Maintain the alloy composition and density; compare laser surface-remelted samples with untreated samples in identical corrosion environments (e.g., 3.5 wt% NaCl) and high-temperature oxidation tests.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: A refined surface microstructure with reduced intermetallic size and improved homogeneity, leading to fewer and less severe microgalvanic couples at the surface.
hypothesis.mechanism: Rapid solidification during laser surface remelting decreases the time available for intermetallic coarsening and phase segregation, yielding a refined, homogeneous surface layer. This layer is less prone to microgalvanic corrosion and, when exposed to high-temperature environments, favours the nucleation of a continuous and adherent protective oxide scale. Although increased surface roughness might be a concern, subsequent minor polishing (if needed) can mitigate any adverse effects.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated samples, the laser remelted surfaces are expected to show reduced corrosion current densities (on a qualitative scale, likely a 20–30% improvement) and a slower oxide scale growth rate with more uniform adherence during high-temperature oxidation tests.
hypothesis.baseline: Alloy surfaces processed solely by conventional induction melting and subsequent slow cooling without additional surface modification.
hypothesis.boundary: The method is effective in the near-surface region (~50–100 µm) and is most beneficial when surface-controlled degradation dominates corrosion and oxidation behavior. The laser parameters must be tuned to avoid excessive roughening or defect creation.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The extent of improvement may be limited to surface phenomena, and potential trade-offs with increased surface roughness or residual stress need careful optimization.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two groups of samples: one with laser surface remelting applied to the top 100 µm and one without. Characterize the surface microstructure using EBSD/TEM to verify grain refinement. Conduct corrosion tests (potentiodynamic polarization and EIS in 3.5 wt% NaCl) and high-temperature oxidation tests (TGA and scale morphology analysis).
measurements: Surface grain size and intermetallic distribution (via EBSD/TEM)
Corrosion parameters (icorr, Rp, Ecorr)
Oxide scale thickness, uniformity, and adhesion quality post-oxidation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If laser-treated samples do not exhibit significant surface grain refinement and fail to show improved corrosion or oxidation performance compared to untreated samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C3

source_paper.title: Corrosion Behavior of MgTiZn and Mg<sub>4</sub>TiZn Alloys After Ball Milling and Subsequent Spark Plasma Sintering.

hypotheses.builds_on: the paper’s observation that Ti-rich intermetallics in the alloy contribute to enhanced passivation, and on earlier reports of region-dependent performance in compositionally graded alloys.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes a deliberate design of a compositional gradient during SPS consolidation to spatially engineer the surface composition, a strategy not explored in the paper, to achieve a selective passivation mechanism.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Engineering a compositional gradient during SPS consolidation that enriches the surface with Ti and Zn while maintaining a Mg-rich core will lead to selective formation of a TiO2-dominated passivation layer at the surface, resulting in improved corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: A non-equilibrium Mg-containing high-entropy alloy with a homogeneous distribution of Mg, Ti, Zn, and other elements as produced by ball milling and conventional SPS.
hypothesis.intervention: Utilize a modified SPS process to create a compositionally graded structure—by layering powder with increased Ti and Zn concentrations near the surface and a Mg-rich composition in the interior.
hypothesis.conditions: Controlled comparison between graded alloys and uniformly mixed alloys, with subsequent testing through potentiodynamic polarization in 0.1 M NaCl and high-temperature oxidation trials (e.g., at 450°C).
hypothesis.structural_mediator: A two-layer microstructure: an outer region rich in Ti and Zn that preferentially oxidizes to form a dense and stable TiO2-dominated passivation film, and an inner Mg-rich core that retains ductility and lower density.
hypothesis.mechanism: The engineered surface enrichment leads to selective oxidation where Ti oxidizes to form TiO2. This oxide is known for its excellent barrier properties against further oxidation and corrosion. The gradient minimizes micro-galvanic coupling within the bulk, while the surface TiO2 layer curtails the ingress of corrosive species, thereby stabilizing both high-temperature oxidation and corrosion behavior.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: The graded alloy is expected to exhibit a significantly lower corrosion current density and a thinner, more adherent oxide scale during high-temperature oxidation compared to homogeneous samples. The improvement is anticipated to be evident through more uniform passivation and reduced localized corrosion.
hypothesis.baseline: Homogeneous Mg-containing high-entropy alloy produced by conventional ball milling and SPS.
hypothesis.boundary: The technique must be applicable to systems with overall densities below 6 g/cm³ and where stable intermetallic compounds naturally form.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the performance improvement is uncertain, as it depends on the effectiveness of the gradient formation and its impact on phase transformations during oxidation.

falsification_experiment.design: Create two groups of samples: one with a compositionally graded structure (Ti and Zn enriched surface) and one with a homogeneous composition. Perform parallel corrosion measurements in 0.1 M NaCl and high-temperature oxidation tests at 450°C. Characterize the oxide layer using XPS and SEM.
measurements: Corrosion current density from potentiodynamic polarization
Thickness and composition of the oxide scale (XPS, SEM)
Uniformity and adherence of the surface oxide layer
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the graded samples do not develop a more TiO2-rich, uniform surface layer and do not show improved corrosion and oxidation resistance relative to the homogeneous counterparts, the hypothesis must be rejected.

hypotheses.label: C5

source_paper.title: First principles-based design of lightweight high entropy alloys.

hypotheses.builds_on: This approach leverages the known sensitivity of Si (and to a lesser degree Mg) on formation energy from the computational study and established principles of laser-induced microsegregation in metals, aiming to engineer an advantageous surface composition that directly influences oxidation and corrosion behavior.
hypotheses.what_is_new: It introduces a novel surface engineering strategy—laser surface remelting—to create a deliberately modified, layered microstructure with enriched Mg and Si near the surface, linking such localized compositional evolution to enhanced high-temperature oxidation resistance and modified corrosion responses, a mechanism not addressed in the original work.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Laser surface remelting of the as‐cast non‐equilibrium Mg-containing HEA will induce localized microstructural refinement and compositional segregation—specifically promoting enrichment of Mg and Si near the surface—which in turn facilitates the formation of a layered, composite oxide (rich in MgO and SiO₂) during high-temperature oxidation and modifies the surface’s corrosion behavior.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: An as‐cast, non‐equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight HEA with a homogeneous, supersaturated solid-solution microstructure.
hypothesis.intervention: Apply pulsed laser surface remelting to the alloy to selectively melt and rapidly resolidify the surface layer.
hypothesis.conditions: Laser parameters (pulse energy, duration, spot size) must be tuned to achieve a shallow remelt depth under an inert atmosphere; following treatment, perform isothermal oxidation testing at 700 °C and standardized corrosion tests in a controlled electrolyte.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: A refined, layered surface structure with localized enrichment of Mg and Si relative to the bulk.
hypothesis.mechanism: The rapid thermal cycle induced by the laser remelting process causes localized melting and rapid resolidification. Due to solute trapping and rapid cooling, elements with different diffusivities such as Mg and Si segregate near the surface. This results in a compositional gradient that, when exposed to high-temperature oxidation, promotes preferential oxidation of the enriched surface layer to form a coherent composite oxide of MgO and SiO₂. The modified surface chemistry also affects local electrochemical potentials, altering corrosion initiation behavior.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated, conventionally cast samples, laser-remelted HEA surfaces will show a measurable enrichment of Mg and Si (as verified by surface analysis techniques), a more uniform and adherent composite oxide scale during high-temperature oxidation (evidenced by lower oxidation weight gain and finer oxide morphology), and distinct corrosion behavior (e.g., altered pit initiation and lower corrosion currents).
hypothesis.baseline: Conventional as‐cast HEA with uniform bulk composition and no specific surface enrichment of any element.
hypothesis.boundary: The laser parameters must be optimized to confine the modification to a surface layer without inducing significant residual stresses or cracking; the mechanism assumes that the altered surface chemistry is retained during subsequent thermal exposures.
hypothesis.uncertainty: Quantitative details regarding the optimal laser processing parameters to achieve the desired elemental segregation and the exact improvement in oxidation/corrosion behavior are not precisely known.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of samples from the same as‐cast alloy: one group undergoes pulsed laser surface remelting under the optimized conditions while the control group receives no laser treatment. Characterize the surface composition using techniques such as XPS or SIMS to verify Mg/Si enrichment. Then subject both groups to isothermal oxidation at 700 °C and standardized corrosion tests (e.g., potentiodynamic polarization), and compare oxide scale morphology and corrosion performance.
measurements: Surface composition profiling (XPS, SIMS)
Microstructural analysis of the remelted layer (SEM, TEM)
Oxidation kinetics (weight gain measurements, oxide scale thickness by SEM/XRD)
Electrochemical corrosion parameters (corrosion current density, pit density)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the laser-remelted samples do not exhibit significant surface enrichment of Mg and Si, or if the subsequent oxidation and corrosion performance shows no improvement (or is worse) compared to the control samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.
